headline: The Leverage Illusion: What a Prize-Winning Paper Actually Found — and What It Didn't
lede: A 2016 Charles H. Dow Award paper by Michael Gayed and Charlie Bilello made a genuinely interesting case that deploying borrowing strategically — only when the market trades above its 200-day moving average — can dramatically outperform unlevered buy-and-hold. The numbers are extraordinary. The caveats are more extraordinary still.
body:
Every few years a piece of financial research escapes the academic circuit and becomes a market meme, its conclusions compressed into a single astonishing figure and its qualifications left behind in the footnotes. Michael A. Gayed and Charles Bilello's 2016 paper — "Leverage for the Long Run: A Systematic Approach to Managing Risk and Magnifying Returns in Stocks," winner of the Charles H. Dow Award from the CMT Association — has completed that journey. The tweet distilling it claims that $10,000 invested in the S&P 500 in 1928 becomes $39 million by 2015 under simple buy-and-hold, while the same stake, rotated into 3x leverage above the 200-day moving average and Treasury bills below it, becomes $28 trillion. The first number is roughly accurate; the second is a significant exaggeration of what the paper actually reports.

According to the paper's own backtested figures — running from October 1928 through October 2015 — a simple buy-and-hold of the S&P 500 Total Return Index grows $10,000 to approximately $19 million, not $39 million. The 3x Leveraged Rotation Strategy (LRS), as the authors term it, produces a terminal value closer to $9 trillion, not $28 trillion. These are still numbers that stagger the imagination, and the paper's core finding — that the 3x LRS outperforms unleveraged buy-and-hold during 80 percent of rolling three-year periods, with smaller maximum drawdowns through the four worst bear markets in U.S. history — holds up as a genuine result. But the tweet nearly trebles the headline figure, and that inflation matters, because the number is already so large as to be operationally meaningless, and inflating it further only hastens the slide into mythology.

The mechanism Gayed and Bilello identify is real and conceptually sound. The 200-day moving average, one of the oldest tools in technical analysis, acts here not as a chart pattern but as a volatility regime indicator. When the broad market trades above that line, it tends to exhibit lower than average forward volatility, higher average daily returns, and longer runs of consecutive positive sessions — precisely the conditions under which leverage compounds favorably rather than destructively. Leverage is the enemy of choppy, mean-reverting markets; it thrives in smooth, trending ones. By switching to three-month Treasury bills whenever the index closes below the 200-day average, the strategy sidesteps roughly 69 percent of recessionary market time, converting that dead capital into a safe-harbor return while waiting for conditions to improve. The Sharpe ratio (the ratio of excess return to volatility, a standard measure of risk-adjusted performance) for the 3x LRS reaches 0.51, compared with 0.30 for unlevered buy-and-hold and 0.27 for constant 2x leverage — confirming that the rotation rule earns its keep even after accounting for annual leverage costs of one percent.

The paper's own authors flag the caveats most likely to reduce the real-world haul. The 1928 start date is, by their admission, "highly favorable" to moving-average rules, because the Great Depression arrives almost immediately thereafter and the strategy's defensive rotation earns its most dramatic returns in exactly the first decade. Strip that out, or begin the backtest from a more neutral moment, and the advantage narrows considerably. More critically, the one-percent annual leverage charge assumed throughout the study is a substantial underestimate for much of the century under review; actual margin borrowing costs for a retail investor in the 1930s or 1970s bore no resemblance to that figure. The 200-day moving average generates roughly five crossovers per year on average, and in choppy tape — think the COVID whipsaw of February through April 2020, or the sideways grind of 2011 — those signals arrive rapidly, each one triggering a full rotation. Transaction costs, bid-ask spreads, and tax events on gains compound across dozens of round-trips and are entirely absent from the model. Academic literature on moving-average timing strategies consistently finds that gross-return outperformance largely evaporates once realistic frictions are applied.

The out-of-sample evidence is, charitably, mixed. Gayed's real-money vehicle, the ATAC Rotation Fund, offers the most direct test of whether the strategy survives contact with live markets. The fund returned 72.5 percent in 2020, capturing the post-COVID surge. But it lost 10.5 percent in 2021, 25.8 percent in 2022, and 2.1 percent in 2023 — three consecutive years of significant underperformance against the S&P 500. Over the five years ending in late 2025, the fund produced a negative annualized return. Its portfolio turnover rate exceeds 1,300 percent per year, the direct real-money consequence of all those 200-day crossings. The pattern is legible: the strategy does exactly what it promises during sharp, well-defined bear markets — it exits — but it pays for that insurance in whipsaw losses and opportunity cost during the long, jagged bull markets that make up most of the calendar.

The volatility-decay argument at the heart of the tweet deserves separate treatment, because it is both the paper's most durable contribution and its most frequently misunderstood. The conventional wisdom holds that leveraged ETFs (exchange-traded funds that reset their leverage daily, targeting two or three times the index's single-day return) decay inevitably over time through a mechanism called volatility drag — the arithmetic-geometric spread that causes compounded returns to fall below the simple-average return when any volatility is present, and that is amplified by leverage. Gayed and Bilello's point is more specific and more defensible: volatility drag is not a property of leverage per se but a property of the volatility environment in which leverage is deployed. In low-volatility trending markets, daily-reset leverage compounds favorably; in high-volatility choppy markets, it destroys capital. Recent academic work, including a 2025 preprint in the arXiv finance series, has confirmed this conditionality — LETF performance depends fundamentally on return autocorrelation, not on leverage alone. The tweet somewhat garbles this into a claim that leveraged ETF decay is a myth outright, which it is not; what is a myth is that the decay is unconditional and inevitable regardless of regime. The regime is everything, and the regime is what the 200-day moving average is trying to identify.

concepts.definition: The performance shortfall that accumulates in a leveraged exchange-traded fund relative to the simple multiple of its underlying index over time. Because a daily-reset leveraged ETF targets a fixed multiple of each day's return (e.g., 3x), the compounded (geometric) return falls below three times the compounded index return whenever volatility is present — a consequence of the mathematical gap between arithmetic and geometric means. The effect is amplified in choppy, mean-reverting markets and reduced in smooth, trending ones. It is sometimes called 'volatility drag' or 'variance drain.'

A technical indicator calculated as the arithmetic average of an asset's closing prices over the previous 200 trading sessions (roughly ten calendar months). It smooths short-term noise and is widely used to distinguish bullish regimes (price above the average) from bearish ones (price below). In the Gayed/Bilello framework, the 200-DMA serves not as a trading signal per se but as a proxy for the volatility regime: markets trading above it tend to exhibit lower forward volatility and longer positive return streaks, conditions favorable to leveraged exposure.

A standard measure of risk-adjusted return, defined as the portfolio's excess return above the risk-free rate divided by the standard deviation of those returns. A higher Sharpe ratio indicates more return earned per unit of volatility borne. It was developed by Nobel laureate William F. Sharpe and is the most commonly used single-number summary of a strategy's efficiency. A Sharpe of 0.5 is considered adequate; above 1.0 is strong.

The specific trading rule proposed in Gayed and Bilello's 2016 paper: hold the S&P 500 with a fixed leverage multiplier (1.25x, 2x, or 3x) when the index closes above its 200-day moving average, and rotate entirely into three-month Treasury bills when it closes below. The strategy generates roughly five rotations per year on average and was backtested from October 1928 through October 2015.

The property of a trading strategy whose performance is critically sensitive to the market environment — the 'regime' — in which it operates. A regime-dependent strategy may show spectacular backtested results over a specific historical sample (e.g., one beginning just before a Great Depression that validated its defensive mechanism) while performing poorly or erratically when regimes shift. Testing for regime dependence typically requires out-of-sample or walk-forward analysis across multiple distinct market environments.

See 'leveraged ETF decay.' In the specific context of the Gayed/Bilello paper, volatility drag is reframed as a conditional risk: not an inherent tax on all leveraged positions, but a function of the volatility level at the time leverage is applied. Low-volatility trending markets generate positive compounding effects; high-volatility choppy markets generate negative ones.

repos.description: Community attempt to replicate the Gayed/Bilello Leverage Rotation Strategy backtest

fact_check: The tweet's '$28 trillion' claim is materially overstated. The Gayed/Bilello paper's actual backtested terminal value for $10,000 invested in 1928 under the 3x Leverage Rotation Strategy is approximately $9 trillion through October 2015 — an enormous figure, but less than one-third of what the tweet asserts. The buy-and-hold baseline is similarly inflated: the paper shows roughly $19 million, not the $39 million the tweet claims. The real figures are spectacular enough; the inflation appears to stem from either a different time horizon, a mis-read of the paper's exhibits, or secondary compression as the claim passed through social media. Separately, the paper's backtested outperformance is substantially eroded by realistic leverage costs, transaction friction from roughly five annual rotations, and the choice of a 1928 start date that placed the Great Depression immediately at the outset — the moment most favorable to the strategy's defensive mechanism. Gayed's live ATAC Rotation Fund, the most direct real-money test, produced negative five-year annualized returns as of late 2025.
